kids-money-shop: Pick Pay, Give change or My shop
Pay: pay the exact price of an item. Give change: you are the shopkeeper and give back the right change. My shop: fill a basket from the shelf and pay.
Tap a note or coin to put it in the tray. Tap one in the tray to take it back. The total is shown in big numbers, so children can watch the amount grow.
Press Pay or Give change. The shop says whether it is right, how much more is needed, and shows an easy way to make the amount.
In My shop, parents and teachers can change the names and prices of the six items, such as to match a real shop at home or a classroom shop day.
tambola-ticket-generator: Type a title, choose a colour and the number of sheets. Each sheet has 6 tickets that together use every number from 1 to 90 once. Press New tickets for a different set.
Download the PDF and print it on A4. Each page is one sheet of six tickets with the title and the prize line.
Open Number caller and press the big button. Each number is shown large, with a traditional call for many numbers, and added to the board. Switch on Voice to hear it read out.
The board shows every number called so far, so anyone can check a claim for Early Five, a line or a Full House.
shadow-explorer-for-kids: Hold the sun and slide it along its path, or use the slider. Low on the left is early morning, the top is noon, and low on the right is evening.
Drag the person, tree or flagpole left or right, or pick a different one. The shadow always starts at the feet.
Press Hide the shadow so I can guess, decide where it will fall, then press Show the shadow to check.
Open Quiz and choose a level. Say which side the shadow falls on, whether it is long or short, or move the sun to make a shadow you are asked for.
addition-with-carrying-for-kids: Choose one of the examples, press the shuffle button for a new one, or open My own numbers and type your own, up to 999.
Press Play, or tap the sum to move one step at a time. The orange line shows the working in numbers, and a small 1 appears above the next column when you carry.
Press You try. Type the answer for each step and press Check. If you get stuck twice, Show me reveals the step.
Press Another sum for a new one. Start with sums that have no carrying, then try carrying once, then twice.
subtraction-with-borrowing-for-kids: Choose one of the examples, press the shuffle button for a new one, or open My own numbers and type your own. The first number must be the bigger one.
Press Play, or tap the sum to move one step at a time. When a column cannot be taken away, the digit next door is crossed out and a new one written, and the orange line shows the working.
Press You try. Type the new numbers after borrowing and then the answer for each column. If you get stuck twice, Show me reveals the step.
Press Another sum. Try sums with no borrowing first, then borrowing once, then 304 − 158 where you must borrow across a zero.
long-multiplication-for-kids: Choose an example, press the shuffle button for a new one, or open My own numbers and type a number up to 999 times a number from 2 to 99.
Press Play, or tap the sum to move one step at a time. The orange line shows the working, such as 7 × 6 = 42 and Write 2, carry 4.
Press You try. Type the answer to each little multiplication, then the digit to write and the number to carry. After two wrong tries, Show me reveals the step.
Choose a sum like 46 × 23. Each digit of the bottom number gets its own row, the second row starts with a 0, and the two rows are added at the end.

kidsMoneyShop.title: Money Shop for Kids
kidsMoneyShop.subtitle: Learn rupee notes and coins by playing shop. Pay the exact price, give change as the shopkeeper, or fill a basket in your own shop with prices you set. Free, private, no sign-up.
faq: What age is the Money Shop for?

It suits children of about 5 to 9, in classes 1 to 4. Easy has prices up to ₹50 in round numbers. Medium goes to ₹200 and Hard goes to ₹500 with odd amounts like ₹37. Start with the level where your child can pay exactly most of the time.
Why do the notes look like plain coloured blocks?
They are play money. Each one is a coloured block with the amount and the words play money, so children learn to tell the amounts by number and colour. They are not copies of real notes.
What is the difference between Pay, Give change and My shop?

In Pay, the child makes an exact amount for an item. In Give change, the customer hands over a note and the child works out and gives back the change, which is the harder skill. In My shop, the child chooses several items, sees the total and pays, and the shop shows the change if they overpay.
Can I set my own prices?
Yes. Open the Parents and teachers section in My shop and change the names and prices of the six items. The changes are saved on your own device. You can put the original prices back at any time.
How should a child work out change?

Count up from the price to the note that was paid. For a ₹35 item paid with ₹50, count ₹5 to make ₹40, then ₹10 to make ₹50, so the change is ₹15. The shop shows an easy way to make the right amount after each answer.
Is it better to use real coins as well?

Yes, if you can. Playing shop with real or toy coins and notes at home helps a lot, and this page is a good way to practise the sums in between. You could use My shop with the prices of your real shelf.
Is anything stored or uploaded?
Nothing is sent to {{siteName}}. Your child's scores are not saved. Only the shop prices you change are remembered, and only on your own device.

kidsTambola.title: Tambola Ticket Generator and Number Caller
kidsTambola.subtitle: Print tambola (housie) tickets, six per sheet using every number from 1 to 90, and call the numbers on screen with a board and optional voice. Free, private, no sign-up.
faq: How are the tickets made?

Each sheet is a book of 6 tickets. Together they use every number from 1 to 90 exactly once. Each ticket has 3 rows and 9 columns with 15 numbers, 5 in each row, and every column holds numbers from its own band (1 to 9, 10 to 19, and so on up to 80 to 90) in rising order. Every ticket has at least one number in each column, like printed tambola tickets.
Are all the tickets different?
Yes. Every time you press New tickets or change the number of sheets, the tickets are made fresh at random. All the sheets in one download are different from each other.
How many tickets should I print?
One sheet has 6 tickets. For a family party, 2 or 3 sheets is plenty. For a kitty party or a society event, print one ticket per person plus a few spare, and cut the sheets into tickets.
What are the usual prizes?

Common prizes are Early Five (the first person to cross off any five numbers), Top Line, Middle Line, Bottom Line and Full House (all 15 numbers). The prize line is printed at the foot of each page, and you can agree your own rules before you start.
How does the number caller work?

Press Call next number. A random number from 1 to 90 that has not been called is shown large, with a traditional call for many numbers such as Two little ducks for 22. The board shows everything called so far. You can undo the last number if you called one by mistake.
Can the caller read the numbers aloud?
Yes, if your browser supports it. Switch on Voice and each new number is spoken. It is off to begin with so that it does not make a noise unexpectedly.
What if the page is closed in the middle of a game?
The numbers called so far are kept on your own device, so you can reopen the page and carry on. Press New game, and then tap again to confirm, to start afresh.
Is anything uploaded?
No. The tickets and the numbers are made in your browser and nothing is sent to {{siteName}}.

kidsShadow.title: Shadow and Sun Explorer for Kids
kidsShadow.subtitle: Drag the sun and see where the shadow falls and how long it is. Hide it to guess first, then take the quiz. Free, private, works on phones.
faq: Why does the shadow fall on the side away from the sun?
A shadow is the place the sun's light cannot reach because something is in the way. The light travels in straight lines from the sun, so the dark patch is always on the opposite side of the object.
Why are shadows long in the morning and evening?
When the sun is low, its rays come in at a slant and the object blocks a long strip of ground. When the sun is high, the rays come almost straight down, so the shadow is short.
Why is there almost no shadow at noon?
At noon the sun is at its highest and shines nearly straight down, so the shadow is only a small patch under the feet. The tool shows noon as a small patch.
What age is it for?
It suits children of about 6 to 10, from class 1 to class 5, when shadows and the sun are taught. Easy asks only which side. Medium adds long or short. Hard asks the child to move the sun.
Is this exactly how the real sun moves?
It is a simple model for learning. It shows the sun rising in the east and setting in the west, and the shadow length from the sun's height. The real path changes with the place and the season.
Is anything uploaded?
No. It all runs in your browser and nothing is saved or sent.

kidsAddition.title: Addition with Carrying for Kids
kidsAddition.subtitle: Watch every carry happen in column addition, then try it yourself with your own numbers. Free, private, works on phones.
faq: What does carrying mean in addition?

When the digits in one column add up to 10 or more, we cannot write the whole number in that column. We write the ones digit and carry the ten to the next column, where it is added with the other digits there.
Why do we carry a 1 and not the whole number?
Because the carried amount is one group of ten. A column holds a single digit. Ten ones make one ten, so we move one group of ten into the tens column and keep the ones that are left.
What is another name for carrying?
Schools also call it regrouping, and some books say "carry over". They all mean the same thing: making a group of ten and moving it to the next column.
What age is this for?
It suits children of about 6 to 9, from class 1 to class 4, when two-digit and three-digit addition is taught. Start with sums with no carrying, then carry once, then carry twice.
How does the You try mode work?

The sum starts hidden. For each step you type the answer, like 8 + 7, and then the digit to write and the number to carry. The page tells you if it is right. After two tries a Show me button reveals the step.
Is my child's work saved or sent anywhere?
No. Everything runs in the browser. Nothing is uploaded or saved.

kidsSubtraction.title: Subtraction with Borrowing for Kids
kidsSubtraction.subtitle: Watch how borrowing works in column subtraction, even across a zero, then try it yourself with your own numbers. Free, private, works on phones.
faq: What does borrowing mean in subtraction?

When the top digit in a column is smaller than the digit to take away, we borrow one group from the column on its left. That group is worth ten of this column, so the top digit gets ten more and the digit on the left goes down by one.
Why does the top digit get 10 more?
One ten is the same as ten ones, and one hundred is the same as ten tens. Borrowing swaps one bigger block for ten smaller ones, so the amount stays exactly the same.
What do we do when the next digit is zero, like 304 − 158?
The zero has nothing to lend, so we go one column further. The hundreds give one hundred, which becomes ten tens. Then one of those tens is lent to the ones. The tens digit ends up as 9.
Is borrowing the same as regrouping?
Yes. Some schools say regrouping or exchanging. They all mean swapping one bigger block for ten smaller ones so the column can be taken away.
What age is this for?
It suits children of about 6 to 9, from class 1 to class 4. Start with sums with no borrowing, then borrow once, then try borrowing across a zero.
Is my child's work saved or sent anywhere?
No. Everything runs in the browser. Nothing is uploaded or saved.

kidsMultiplication.title: Long Multiplication for Kids
kidsMultiplication.subtitle: Watch long multiplication one digit at a time, with every carry, then try it yourself with your own numbers. Free, private, works on phones.
faq: How does long multiplication work?

You multiply the top number by one digit of the bottom number at a time, starting with the ones. Each little multiplication gives a digit to write and sometimes a number to carry. With a two-digit bottom number you get two rows, which are added together at the end.
Why do we put a 0 at the start of the second row?

The second digit of the bottom number is in the tens place, so it really means ten times that digit. Starting the row with a 0 moves every digit one place to the left, which is the same as multiplying by ten.
What do we carry in multiplication?
When one little multiplication makes a number of 10 or more, we write the ones digit and carry the tens digit. We add the carried number to the next multiplication in the row, for example 4 × 3 + 1.
What should my child know first?
Children should know their times tables up to 9 and be happy with addition with carrying. If a times table is slow, the You try mode is a good place to practise the one that is hard.
What age is this for?
It suits children of about 8 to 11, from class 3 to class 5. Start with a one-digit multiplier such as 47 × 6, then try two digits such as 46 × 23.
Is my child's work saved or sent anywhere?
No. Everything runs in the browser. Nothing is uploaded or saved.

sections.heading: Why playing shop works
paragraphs: Money is hard to learn from a book, because the answer depends on handling it: which note, which coin, how many. Children learn it quickly when they pay, count and give change themselves. A play shop makes the sums feel real, and being the shopkeeper makes children think about change in the right direction.
Five to ten minutes at a time is enough. Stop on a success.

sections.heading: A good order to learn
paragraphs: Start with paying exact amounts using whole tens, then use fives and ones. Next, practise reading prices and adding two items together in My shop. Then move to change, starting with small differences such as paying ₹20 for a ₹15 item, and building up to ₹100 and ₹500 notes.
The Easy level keeps to round prices, so children focus on the idea. Hard adds amounts like ₹37 that need coins.

sections.heading: Counting up to make change
paragraphs: Shopkeepers rarely subtract. They count up from the price to the amount paid. If something costs ₹65 and a ₹100 note is paid, you say 65, then add ₹5 to reach 70, ₹10 to reach 80, and ₹20 to reach 100. The change is ₹5 + ₹10 + ₹20 = ₹35. Practise saying it aloud.

sections.heading: Use it with real life
paragraphs: Let your child look at real prices in a shop, then put them into My shop and play at home. Give a small amount of pocket money and let them plan what to buy. Real choices make the maths matter.

sections.heading: How tambola is played
paragraphs: Tambola, also called housie, is a number game for any number of players. Each player gets a ticket. A caller draws numbers from 1 to 90 one at a time, and players cross off the numbers they have. The first to complete a prize pattern shouts and claims it.
The usual prizes are Early Five, Top Line, Middle Line, Bottom Line and Full House. You can agree extra prizes before you start, such as the four corners.

sections.heading: Why a proper ticket set matters
paragraphs: Tickets made by picking random numbers can contain a lot of duplicates between players, and some can be much luckier than others. A printed book of 6 tickets uses every number from 1 to 90 exactly once, so every number called is on exactly one ticket in the book. That makes the game fair and gives a clear winner.

sections.heading: Running the game
paragraphs: Give each player a ticket and something to mark it, such as a pen or counters. Use the Number caller on a phone, a tablet or a laptop connected to a screen so that everyone can see the numbers, or read them out loud. The board lets you check a claim by looking at which numbers have been called.
For young children, call the numbers slowly and show the number on the screen. Tambola is a good way to practise recognising numbers up to 90.

sections.heading: Planning a party
paragraphs: For a family party, print 2 or 3 sheets. For a kitty party or a society gathering, print about one ticket per person and cut the sheets with scissors. Small prizes keep it fun, and a few spare tickets help latecomers. Put the host's name in the line at the bottom so the tickets look personal.

sections.heading: What children learn from it
paragraphs: A shadow depends on three things: where the light is, where the object is, and how high the light is. Moving the sun and the person themselves lets a child see each one separately, which a textbook picture cannot.
The dashed line is the sun ray that just touches the top of the head. It ends exactly where the shadow ends, so children can see that the shadow is the part of the ground that the ray cannot reach.

sections.heading: A good way to use it
paragraphs: First let the child play freely for a few minutes. Then use Hide the shadow so I can guess, ask them to say the answer aloud, and show it. Finish with the Easy quiz, and move to Medium when most answers are right.
Afterwards, go outside in the morning and afternoon and look at a real shadow. Ask the child to point to where the sun is and where the shadow falls.

sections.heading: Ideas to try
paragraphs: Ask when the shadow would be shortest and when longest. Compare the person, the tree and the flagpole at the same sun position. Ask which way the shadow points at sunrise and at sunset, and why.

sections.heading: What carrying really is
paragraphs: Column addition adds one place at a time, starting with the ones. A column can only hold one digit, so when 8 and 7 make 15, the 15 has to be split. Ten of the ones are bundled into one ten, and that ten is moved to the tens column. What is left, 5, stays in the ones column.

Children often learn this as a rule: write the 5, carry the 1. This page shows why the rule works. The orange line shows each step in numbers, and the small 1 that appears above the next column is the bundle of ten that moved.

sections.heading: A good order to practise in
paragraphs: Begin with sums that need no carrying, like 23 + 14, so the idea of adding column by column is clear. Then try a sum that carries once, like 27 + 15. After that, carry twice, like 58 + 67, where a carry from the ones makes the tens carry again. Finish with three-digit sums such as 146 + 278.
Use Watch first, then You try. If your child is stuck twice, Show me reveals the step so they can keep going.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to look for
paragraphs: Forgetting to add the carried 1 is the most common mistake. In the You try mode the carried 1 is shown in the sum, such as 1 + 5 + 6, so it is not forgotten. Another is writing both digits of a two-digit column total. Remind your child that each column keeps one digit.

sections.heading: What borrowing really is
paragraphs: In 52 − 27, the ones column has 2 and we need to take away 7. We cannot, so one ten is taken from the 5 and swapped for ten ones. The 5 becomes 4 and the 2 becomes 12. Now 12 − 7 = 5, and 4 − 2 = 2, so the answer is 25.
The total amount has not changed. One ten and ten ones are the same amount, so the borrowing only changes how the number is written. The crossed-out digits on the page show exactly that.

sections.heading: Borrowing across a zero
paragraphs: The hardest case is a zero in the middle, like 304 − 158. The tens digit is 0, so it has nothing to give. Borrow from the hundreds first: 3 becomes 2 and the 0 becomes 10. Then borrow one ten from that 10 to give the ones: the 10 becomes 9 and the 4 becomes 14. The page shows each of these changes one after the other.

sections.heading: A good order to practise in
paragraphs: Start with sums that need no borrowing, like 48 − 23. Then borrow once, like 52 − 27. Then try 91 − 58 and three-digit sums such as 421 − 186. Leave borrowing across a zero until the rest feels easy.
Use Watch first, then You try. If your child is stuck twice, Show me reveals the step so they can keep going.

sections.heading: What long multiplication really does
paragraphs: Long multiplication breaks a big multiplication into small ones that fit a times table. In 47 × 6, the 7 ones times 6 make 42, so 2 is written in the ones place and 4 tens are carried. The 4 tens times 6 make 24, plus the carried 4 makes 28, and the answer is 282.
The orange line on the page shows each small multiplication as it happens, and the small orange number above a digit is the carry waiting to be added.

sections.heading: Multiplying by a two-digit number
paragraphs: For 46 × 23, you multiply 46 by 3 first, which gives 138. Then you multiply 46 by the 2 tens, which really means 20, so the row starts with a 0 and reads 920. Adding 138 and 920 gives 1058.
Children often forget the 0 at the start of the second row. The page writes it first and says so, so the pattern becomes familiar.

sections.heading: A good order to practise in
paragraphs: Start with a one-digit multiplier and no carrying, such as 23 × 4. Then try a carry, such as 47 × 6, and a three-digit number, such as 156 × 7. When those feel easy, move to two digits, such as 34 × 12 and 46 × 23.
Use Watch first, then You try. Slow times tables are the most common reason for mistakes, so if the same small multiplication keeps going wrong, practise that table on its own.
